item.title: Dutch woman living in Nepal found alive after surviving floods
item.description:
Dutch woman living in Nepal found alive after surviving floods

September 2, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch foreign office has made contact with a woman living in Nepal who had been reported missing in the wake of last week’s devastating floods, which have killed more than 1,100 people.

Foreign affairs minister Tom Berendsen said there had been “good news” as he spoke to reporters during a meeting of EU foreign ministers in Ireland.

The woman is one of three Dutch nationals who were known to be in Nepal when a glacier in the Himalaya region collapsed last Wednesday, causing water and mud to surge down the Bhote Koshi river and wipe out villages in the Rawusa border region with Tibet.

She was in the Himalaya region when the disaster struck, but has reached the Nepalese capital Kathmandu, where she contacted the foreign ministry.

A spokesman said the government was still “very concerned about the fate of the two other Dutch nationals”, 29-year-old Christiaan Berghuis from Nijkerk and 51-year-old Maaike Moolhuijsen from Haarlem.

They were on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, a sacred Tibetan mountain, when the floods hit. The group of 80 pilgrims were believed to be in an immigration office that was in the path of the floodwaters.

item.title: Cheap Chinese parcels to the Netherlands fall 46% after EU levy
item.description:
Cheap Chinese parcels to the Netherlands fall 46% after EU levy

September 2, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The number of small parcels arriving in the Netherlands from outside the EU fell by 46% in July and August compared with the previous six months, according to customs figures presented to parliament. It is the first clear sign that a new €3 import charge is changing the flow of cheap goods from China.

The drop was revealed by Eelco Eerenberg, the junior finance minister responsible for customs, during a debate in parliament on Tuesday.

Around one million such parcels were arriving in the Netherlands each day before the change, 80% to 90% of them from Chinese platforms such as Shein, Temu and AliExpress.

Since July 1, a new EU-wide charge of €3 has applied to parcels worth up to €150 sent from outside the bloc, which were previously exempt from import duties. The fee is levied per type of product rather than per parcel, so an order containing several different items can be charged more than once.

Customs officials say online retailers are already changing how they operate, moving away from sending millions of individual packages and instead importing goods in bulk to store in warehouses inside the EU before shipping them on to shoppers. The same shift has been seen in France and Belgium.

“The figures give a first indication that fewer loose parcels are going straight to the consumer,” Nanette van Schelven, director-general of the Dutch customs service, told broadcaster NOS, “which makes it easier for us to check whether products are safe.”

A single large shipment is easier to screen for unsafe or banned goods, she said, than a constant stream of separate parcels.

The Dutch share
The charge raised about €134 million in import duties in July alone, of which roughly a quarter went to the Dutch treasury. Customs duties are collected as an EU revenue source: member states keep a share to cover the cost of collection and pass the rest to Brussels.

The Netherlands had drawn up plans for a national surcharge of its own on cheap parcels but dropped them in January, choosing to rely on the EU charge after France and Belgium shelved similar schemes and Brussels brought its levy forward.

item.title: Riot police break up protest against refugee shelter in Zeeland
item.description:
Riot police break up protest against refugee shelter in Zeeland

September 2, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Riot police had to disperse a crowd of around 300 people who staged a protest against plans to set up an emergency shelter for 150 asylum seekers.

Councillors were trapped inside the town hall in Tholen, Zeeland, after demonstrators gathered outside with banners during a meeting to discuss the proposed site.

Police said riot squad officers were sent in “to restore public order as quickly as possible” after some of the protesters were accused of inciting violence.

The council wants to accommodate 150 refugees in a building on Postweg for a maximum of two and a half years to meet its obligations under the so-called “spreading law” (spreidingswet), which requires all municipalities to share the responsibility of housing asylum seekers.

Mayor Marleen Sijbers told councillors not to leave the building until they were given the all-clear by police.

Police dogs and a helicopter were also used to clear the crowd outside the town hall by 11pm. Police have not said if any arrests were made.

item.title: Justice minister warns of “unprecedented” violence after attack
item.description:
Justice minister warns of “unprecedented” violence after attack

September 2, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Justice minister David van Weel has called the violence in the Gelderland village of Overasselt “unprecedented” for the Netherlands, after dozens of armed men shot a man dead and opened fire on police in the early hours of Tuesday.

Dozens of young men moving through a village armed and immediately shooting at police was, he said, something the country had never seen before. Van Weel said it was probably international gangs settling scores – “drug cartels, mafia” that operate across borders.

Both Het Parool and De Telegraaf have cited sources reporting that the attack grew out of a dispute over a large shipment of cocaine tied to the organisation of Jos “Bolle Jos” Leijdekkers, the fugitive regarded as the Netherlands’ most wanted drug lord.

According to Het Parool, figures in the criminal world believe the group came to recover part of a missing cocaine shipment, which would explain the number of men involved.

Residents of Overasselt, who had been told to stay indoors during a day-long manhunt, were allowed back out on Tuesday evening. Police said there was no sign that any suspects were still in or around the village, though extra patrols were deployed overnight and the investigation is ongoing.

Officers confirmed that a 51-year-old man from nearby Wijchen was shot dead – reportedly a security guard hired by the household that was targeted. Two police officers were seriously injured, one of them at one point in a life-threatening condition, though both are now out of danger.

A total of 34 people were arrested at various locations around the country, among them nationals of Belgium, France and Algeria as well as the Netherlands.

Van Weel would not say who was behind the attack, and the public prosecution department has declined to comment on any potential links while the investigation continues.

The targeted property has a long history of drug-related incidents. A drug lab was found there after a fire in 2019, and the same address was shot at with an AK-47 last year. One of its residents is appealing a four-year sentence for drug trafficking, according to broadcaster NOS.

Van Weel rejected the suggestion that the Netherlands had become a “narco-state”, where drugs gangs have free rein, but acknowledged that criminal networks such as those of Leijdekkers and the convicted crime boss Ridouan Taghi had taken root in the country and are benefiting from Dutch financial and logistical facilities.

item.title: Minister sent death threats over plans to shoot “problem wolves”
item.description:
Minister sent death threats over plans to shoot “problem wolves”

September 2, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Junior agriculture minister Silvio Erkens says he has has received death threats after bringing new rules making it easier for provincial and local governments to shoot wolves that pose a danger to people.

Erkens told MPs that local authorities needed more powers to drive away wolves that had lost their fear of humans, with shooting a last resort to deal with so-called “problem wolves”.

He faced criticism in parliament on Tuesday for announcing the measures in July before they could be debated, as well as for his comments in an interview about the shooting of a wolf known as Bram in December 2025.

“The world is on fire, all sorts of things are going on and at the same time people in our country are organising funerals for Bram the wolf. Totally out of touch with the world,” Erkens told the Telegraaf.

Bram, officially designated wolf GW3237m, became a cause célèbre for animal welfare campaigners after Utrecht province gave a local hunting organisation a licence to kill him last July.

It followed a number of incidents in which the wolf had approached humans, including an attack on a child. Bram was shot dead last December after campaigners lost a court battle to have the permit revoked.

14 packs

Erkens also criticised a report by scientists at Wageningen University, who said the Netherlands’ wolf population should be allowed to grow both for legal reasons and to benefit the ecosystem.

He said there was “not a single realistic scenario in which you’d want 56 wolf packs”. Currently there are 14 packs established in the country, with more than 100 wolves altogether.

The return of the animals to the Netherlands a decade ago has sharply divided opinions, with right-wing and rural parties calling for stronger measures to cull their numbers while progressive parties have said they should be protected.

Under Erkens’ rules, a wolf becomes a “problem wolf” if they attack people, react aggressively rather than running away, or attack horses or cattle more than once in a two-week period.

Local authorities then have a range of options to drive off the wolf, including shooting them with paintball guns, with killing them as a last resort. “I would hope that all of us would draw a red line if a child is attacked by a wolf,” he said.

item.title: “Grey divorce” on the rise among the Dutch over-60s
item.description:
“Grey divorce” on the rise among the Dutch over-60s

September 2, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The number of couples divorcing in the Netherlands is still falling, but a growing share of those who do split are over 60 – a trend sometimes called “grey divorce”.

Some 24,555 marriages ended in divorce in 2025, according to national statistics office CBS, down from 30,729 in 2018. The decline has been going for more than a decade. Fewer people are marrying in the first place, and those who do tend to stay together longer.

Older couples are the exception. Divorces among the under-60s have dropped since 2014, but among people over 60 they have gone up, and their share of all divorces has climbed from around 8% a decade ago to about 13% last year.

Hundreds of couples now divorce after 40 years or more together, including some who separate after a 50-year anniversary, which was almost unheard of at the turn of the century.

Relationship therapists link the shift to changing attitudes, with divorce more widely accepted than it was a generation ago, and to the moment when children leave home or retirement approaches and long-married partners find they have little left in common.

There is a knock-on effect on housing. Many older people who split up choose to live apart together rather than move in with a new partner, keeping two homes between them and freeing up fewer properties on an already tight market.

item.title: Cabinet to scrap welfare cuts in revised budget deal – RTL
item.description:
Cabinet to scrap welfare cuts in revised budget deal – RTL

September 1, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch government has scrapped most of its planned cuts to social security as it tries to attract opposition support for next year’s budget, RTL Nieuws has reported.

The cabinet will also delay raising the excess charge for health insurance by a year and invest €1.5 billion in mitigating the impact of inflation, particularly rising energy prices, on spending power.

The deal was the outcome of protracted negotiations between the three coalition partners, D66, VVD, and CDA, which ran through the weekend and most of Monday as the party leaders stretched the deadline to send the draft budget to the Council of State.

RTL Nieuws said it had seen leaked details of the budget proposals, which will not be formally announced for another two weeks when finance minister Eelco Heinen presents it to parliament.

The U-turn on welfare spending is a blow for the right-wing VVD, which had earlier said it would not compromise on the €6.5 billion worth of cuts to incapacity benefit, unemployment payments and substitute pay for new mothers on maternity leave.

Another plan in the coalition agreement to save €2.8 billion by increasing the retirement age in step with life expectancy, rather than by eight months for every extra year, has also been cancelled, as announced earlier by social security minister Hans Vijlbrief.

Heinen and prime minister Rob Jetten had spent the last two weeks trying to do a deal with opposition parties in advance to get their support for the budget, as the coalition is 10 seats short of a majority in the lower house and 16 seats short in the Senate.

But those talks ended without agreement as the three coalition parties struggled to agree among themselves about what concessions they should make to opposition groups on the left and right. Ministers will now have to find the votes when the budget plans go through parliament during the autumn.

Jetten’s D66 party and the Christian Democrats (CDA) reportedly wanted to scale back welfare cuts to appeal to the largest opposition party, the left-wing Progressief Nederland (Pro), while the VVD preferred a package that addressed the demands of right-wing parties such as JA21, with more tax cuts and less welfare spending.

item.title: Far-right TV show editor Niemöller leaves after Hitler remarks
item.description:
Far-right TV show editor Niemöller leaves after Hitler remarks

September 1, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Joost Niemöller is stepping down as editor-in-chief of far-right broadcaster Ongehoord Nederland (ON), weeks after he said on air that Adolf Hitler had put certain things “very well”.

The broadcaster said the immediate reason was a “difference of view about the editorial direction and recent programming”, according to director-general Peter Vlemmix. Its statement, reported by NOS, runs to two sentences and does not mention the item that set off weeks of criticism.

In the late-July broadcast, Niemöller said there were “certain things of Hitler’s” he agreed with, aside from the Nazi leader’s antisemitism.

Co-presenter Raisa Blommestijn also backed a statement, put to the pair after a clip of a Hitler speech referring to Jewish people, that a cosmopolitan elite was inherently hostile to ordinary people. Both said they did not share all of Hitler’s ideology.

Media minister Rianne Letschert called the broadcast “terrible, distasteful, hurtful and unnecessary”, and the ombudsman for the public broadcasters logged dozens of complaints. The cabinet is examining whether ON can be forced out of the public broadcasting system, and Letschert has said a decision will come “very soon”.

Ongehoord Nederland joined the public broadcasting system in 2022 and has been reprimanded and sanctioned several times for breaching journalistic rules. Niemöller became editor-in-chief about 18 months ago.

item.title: Three Dutch nationals remain missing after deadly Nepal floods
item.description:
Three Dutch nationals remain missing after deadly Nepal floods

September 1, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Rescue workers in Nepal are still trying to trace three Dutch nationals among more than 4,000 people reported missing since the devastating floods that swept through the border region with Tibet last week.

They include two tourists, 29-year-old Christiaan Berghuis from Nijkerk and 51-year-old Maaike Moolhuijsen from Haarlem, who were on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, a sacred Tibetan mountain, when the disaster struck.

Their names were confirmed by the family support organisation Names de Familie. The third missing person is a Dutch woman who emigrated to Nepal, the foreign affairs ministry said.

The two visitors were part of a group of 80 people who were travelling from Kathmandu to Mount Kailash when a glacier in the Himalaya collapsed on Wednesday morning, causing the Bhote Koshi river to burst its banks and flood a large area with water and mud.

A spokesman for the Isha Foundation, which organised the trip, told RTL Nieuws the immigration office where the travellers were waiting at the time appeared to have been inundated.

Death toll passes 1,000

“At the moment nothing is known about the conditions of the people who were in the immigration office,” the spokesman said. “We are in constant contact with their families and are supporting them in every way possible.

“The last contact we had with our volunteer who was in charge of the group was around nine minutes before the flood happened.”

The Isha foundation was set up in 1992 by Jaggi Vasudev, an Indian yoga teacher better known by the name of Sandhguru.

A spokesman for the foreign affairs ministry said: “Their families in the Netherlands have been unable to contact them. The fear is that they were in the affected area at the moment of the flood.”

The death toll from the floods passed 1,000 on Tuesday as rescue workers continued to pull bodies from the water further downstream.

Altogether nearly 4,000 people are still unaccounted for in Nepal, as well as 546 in Tibet. They include around 900 hydropower workers who have been trapped in flooded tunnels for nearly a week.

item.title: Amsterdam taxi drivers launch app to rival Uber
item.description:
Amsterdam taxi drivers launch app to rival Uber

September 1, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A group of Amsterdam taxi drivers has launched a rival booking app to try and loosen Uber’s grip on the city’s cab market, amid long-running disputes over employee status, wages and workers’ rights. The founders claim nearly 1,300 drivers have already signed up.

The app, NLCabs, was set up by driver Mostapha Ahidar and co-founder Ivo van Leeuwen, who told Het Parool they were tired of watching a US monopoly control the terms of their trade. It works the same as Uber: passengers order a ride through the app and nearby drivers pick them up.

The difference, the founders say, is the cut. NLCabs takes a 3% commission from drivers, which Ahidar said was only what the platform needs to keep running. Uber’s commission is variable and can rise beyond half the fare, according to the drivers, though the company does not publish its rates.

“We are treated like children by Uber,” one driver told the paper. “We have absolutely no room for negotiation.”

Years of friction
The launch comes after years of conflict between Uber and Dutch drivers, much of which has gone through courts and regulators.

In August, the data protection authority (AP) fined Uber €825 million for deactivating drivers’ accounts through automated systems, without proper human review or explanation – the second-largest penalty ever issued under EU privacy law. Uber is appealing and has called the fine disproportionate.

That followed a €290 million fine in 2024 for sending drivers’ data to the US, a record at the time. Both cases originally stemmed from complaints by French drivers.

Employee or entrepreneur
In January, an Amsterdam appeal court ruled that Uber drivers cannot all be treated as employees, overturning a 2021 judgment that had put them on the payroll. The FNV trade union, which launched the case, said it was weighing a Supreme Court appeal.

Many drivers work almost exclusively through Uber and have little way of finding fares without it.

NLCabs is live but has only a few hundred downloads on Google Play, and the founders said they know shifting a habit as ingrained as opening Uber will be hard. They plan to expand across the Netherlands.
